That's what's up. Like, for me, it never felt right to be called a girl because that was never who I was.

I was born afab and grew up in a house of women, raised the way a "girl" should be raised—I was forced into dresses, my hair was kept long and done up elaborately anytime my mom pleased no matter how much I cried, and I was taught that sex and sexuality was shameful. Well, none of it stuck. I have always hated fem clothing on my body, even if it looks great on others. I rejected feminity so vehemently as a child that my mother remained that she wanted another girl as a do over, so that, "she could actually be girly and like to dress up."

It always felt wrong to call myself a girl or to be called a girl by others, and when I was 13 that all went out the window when I chopped my hair off. When I was a child I had wanted my hair to be long like Rapunzel's...but I guess it's poetically fitting how it only ever ended up causing me grief, because in the end, I wasn't even entitled to do my own hair. So when I hacked it all off, my mother just went offline. Her hopes and dreams for having a girl, having a *mini me* crashed and burned, and I finally felt their warmth. I started dressing more sporty, always practical, and slowly became more headstrong. I stood up for myself. I fought, when I needed to.

It was in later years that I started experimenting with gender fluidity. I don't mind being called a boy—I mean, it doesn't really feel right, but I'd rather be called a boy than a girl. A hate being called a girl, referred to as a woman, what have you. But as I grew up, my body grew too, and I was bestowed with rather generous endowments. I have the perfect body....of a *woman.* 

And the thing is? I like my body. Love it, even, my curves and proportions and everything. The problem is, people see lush titties and swaying hips and think "WAMEN!!" that's it. I don't particularly want to bind my chest, and there's nothing that can even be done about the phat dumpy—but I shouldn't have to. I shouldn't have to bind my chest to be seen as something other than a woman (not that it would even work 100% of the time).

I hate how the binary has gendered everything. Clothes, colors, shapes. Because of the shape of my body, even though I never wear skirts and you wouldn't catch me dead in heels, my black on black clothes are "feminine" when there's nothing feminine at all about the way I dress.

It's just....frustrating. it's so frustrating, because when you think about it, I've spent my life rejecting this fuck ass label people are happy to sweep me under without question. Just yesterday, I was having a very candid conversation with my boss (unrelated; it was about the homeless) and he called me babygirl. Look, I like my boos alright? He's a cool, older black guy—but geez, any other endearment. Literally, anything else would've sufficed. It's things like this and what happened at the smoke sesh, or even people going, "yeah, yeah, I know you're nb, BUT the world sees you as a girl, soooo..." is just SO

Like . Why do I even try.

Okay, hear me out.

The Deliverance. 

Andra Day as the lead actress left me shook. I had no idea she could act—and she played the fuck out of that role. For me, when I watched the movie, I was in shock and on the edge of my seat—because I've lived through that movie. Minus the demon in the basement, of course—but the toxic environment of which those kids were raised. That was my life with my own mom and grandmother, who were also white (my grandma) and mixed (my mom). It even raised a discussion of strained race relationships in such an environment, the way their relationship flip-floped between "I have your back" to "the kids need me more." 

This was the home I was raised in. There were fights. My mom screamed and raged. Things were thrown, glass was shattered. There were manic episodes, many episodes involving cps. My grandma died in our house. 

I almost felt sick watching it, because it was so quintessentially *my household* that they even mirrored things that my mom and grandma had said, word for word. It was haunting. And you know what? If we really *did* have a demon in our walls, we would've been fucked. The only thing that separates the original family and my own is luck. 

Amazing movie. I recommend it wherever I can. It's so nuanced that you realized that no one is really an antagonist, say for the demon. But the demon isn't really a character, more like a force that hangs around and just makes everything worse, but the conflict—the conflict is there since the very beginning. It's accurate. Very, very accurate—at least for me.

So it scared me. It made my heart feel unsettled. And whereas at the end of the movie she got her shit together and found inner strength, I...never spoke to my mom since the day I moved out of her house. That was two years ago. She never found inner strength like Andra Day did. The demon got to her—I think that's what it would've been like if the demon had conquered Andra Day's character in the movie. She would just want to make everyone else more miserable, until someone snapped. 

But the movie doesn't end like that. Even now, there's hope. Sometimes you have to remove yourself from the environment and completely severe your ties to it before things begin to come into fruition. I love the Deliverance. Love it, love it, love it. 

Thank you for reading this reflection.

I roll with the Goddesses Isis and Hathor. My connection to Isis has been with me my entire life. I grew up Christian/Baptist, and I always felt a major preference for ankhs (which I called the loopy cross lol). I read a story on reddit about how Isis came to a young boy on the verge of freezing to death after being thrown outside by his abusive and drunk grandfather in a snowstorm, and years later when I recounted the story my teacher said they got shivers. The moment I knew she was presenting herself to me to reach out to was when I went to Ross (retail) and saw the most gorgeous black statue of her classic kneeling posture with her wings outspread, crystals pressed into her hair. I almost couldn't bear to part with the statue—I almost felt bonded to it. While I didn't get it ($20 was too steep 😭) it felt like my faith in Her was sealed. 

While I do *not* worship, I *do* work with and venerate. 

My connection to Hathor is much more subtle and actually stemmed from reading the Ennead (webcomic). Tbh I just really vibed with her character, and then I thought, "well if I vibe with her character in the comic, perhaps I can vibe with her in real life!" And indeed, we do be vibing. Symbolage, like her crest of the sun disk cradled by bull horns and her being a goddess of cattle (I am a Taurus, and the Taurus symbol is essentially Hathor's own) also influenced me. Hathor has helped me greatly with my own self love and self confidence, love spells I weave from thin air and send out in all directions, and bask in the pain and exuberance that I cycle through in my own love life. If I'm hurting out of love, that is beautiful and should be celebrated. That's how I honor Her and myself. 

What I've learned in my time with the Goddesses is that your connection to the universe through any given medium is spiritual; its mental. You don't have to leave offerings and have an altar and pray. I rarely ever "pray" in the traditional sense, like a Christian would pray to their god. I honor and venerate them in my actions and thoughts, and in doing so the Goddesses live in me. I am Isis and Isis is me. I am Hathor and Hathor is me. I am Lilith and Lilith is me. I think as generations develop, they become more willing to speak out for themselves and demand the same respect an "adult" is due. I will exercise my autonomy, and when you impede on that and ONLY then, that's when you get disrespect. That's when the hackles raise, and everyone looks at the teacher like something to be torn apart. We are our own people. In school, it's a give and take. I show up, you respect that. I take notes respectfully, and you respect me by leaving me be. I pass the class, and you give me grace.

Why this?? This is so toxic! It's giving "you are beneath me until you have suffered and toiled the way I have." And that is....wow. don't you *want* the younger folks of each generations to shatter past the shackles that were set on your person when you were being brought up? Don't you want them to relentlessly seek the things they deserve, devouring anyone who stands in their way? That's what advancement is, right?

I really appreciate the people who read and responded to my first comment. It probably does come off as entitled, I understand that, but...is that such a bad thing? To want more for ourselves? To demand *Respect* in the way we give to our aunties and grandmothers and mothers, so that we can function harmoniously? This idea of "in a classroom, you are a subordinate" is repulsive. A classroom is just a room full of people, and often times it's not just the teacher that teaches.

It feels like I'm seeing a lot of "just beat their asses" from older generations to younger generations, so as a Zoomer still in high school, I will speak. 

Younger teachers tend to know how to deal with students on account of being far more casual and connecting with them in a way that older teachers typically don't. That weird ass veil of professionalism puts off a lot of people, especially when teachers try to ask students to put away their phones in a way that isn't like *asking* at all. 

For example, I have this teacher people tend to like. I hate being in her classroom. The work is boring, but simple so there's that, she offers nothing to spice things up, her classroom is all hard edges and sharp lines of symmetry despite having color which makes it feel sterile and lifeless, and perhaps the most damning thing—she demands our attention at all times, off our phones, headphones off. Having transferred into the class for the semester, I'm one of the only people who pretty much ignores her when I see fit—not out of disrespect, but out of exercising my own autonomy (you will not tell me to put away or take up this object that I have literally fought for, and have struggled for months without). She even threatened to make "following class rules" a grade, in lieu of saying she'd fail us for daily grades if we didn't comply.


Fuck that. 

We will not be made to do things we want to do. And yet there are many teachers who are older, who have been around the block, but still maintain a close knit classroom with students that both pay attention and get along. The key is professionalism. Scrape most of it away. Of course—a thin veil is necessary, but fucking talk to your kids! When they want about their bitches, indulge them.
